source.title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy

record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that raw neuron coordinates in language models can mix unrelated features, and presents its own evaluations of SAE features as evidence that learned features can also remain polysemantic or redundant. It does not directly audit neuron poles.
record.gate_note: No raw neuron poles or neuron explanations are measured. The paper's DAME, redundancy, and larger-model results concern SAE features; cited neuron-study results are not the paper's own results. The paper also gives a conceptual argument that neuron-level attribution can be ambiguous under superposition.
record.test_reason: Every result concerns SAE features, not raw neurons or neuron poles. These include DAME, redundancy, synthetic SAEs and public Qwen3/Gemma SAE panels. The paper treats neuron polysemanticity under superposition as a premise (Section 2.1, citing Elhage et al.) and gives no neuron-level measurement. Its neuron numbers (Bills et al. 0.33% of GPT-2 XL neurons scoring ≥0.8; Templeton et al. 25% of neurons highly relevant) are cited results, not its own. It therefore neither tests nor uses any version. The reader's T5 overstates the paper: its argument against neuron units is a generic restatement of superposition, not results or a specific argument aimed at any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors conclude that SAE features can look monosemantic under standard metrics while the most dominant features are less interpretable and more redundant. They recommend dominance-stratified evaluation before using SAEs for attribution or circuit tracing. They state that the larger-model checks are limited and do not establish scale invariance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates SAE features using dominance-stratified, held-out three-example activation ranking and decoder similarity. It does not reproduce an audit of neuron poles or the cited neuron-explanation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE-feature results vary by SAE architecture and model family. DAME Q1 deficits were not significant for Gated and JumpReLU in the main architecture comparison; the authors attribute this possibly to high L0 from default sparsity hyperparameters. Larger-model deficit percentages vary by model. Judge, explanation-budget, and firing-frequency-matched checks are also reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 600+ SAEs, the most dominant SAE-feature quartile gets lower held-out three-way ranking accuracy than Q2–Q4 (61.8% vs 64.1%). The deficit is significant in 5 of 7 architectures and not significant for Gated and JumpReLU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In SAE dictionaries, the most dominant features are less predictable from their explanations than less dominant features. The size of the gap depends on architecture and effective sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: Public BatchTopK SAEs for Qwen3-8B/14B/32B and Gemma Scope SAEs for Gemma-2-9B show a Q1 token-DAME deficit in 41.7–75% of evaluated SAEs. These shares count the direction of the difference, not significance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The dominance-linked explanation deficit of SAE features appears in some SAEs of larger models, but not uniformly.

fits_no_version.finding: On two SAEs with a DAME Q1 deficit (−11.83 and −9.50 pp), a feature-uniform binary AutoInterp assay shows no gap (+0.13 and +0.35 pp) (Appendix J.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Binary, feature-uniform automated scoring can hide dominance-conditioned explanation failures in SAE features.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: The main benchmark is primarily models in the 70M–2.7B parameter range. Larger-model checks cover limited model, layer, and SAE-family combinations and do not establish scale invariance. Monosemanticity is assessed using an LLM judge and remains a proxy; the authors note dependence on the judge, prompting, validation construction, concept granularity, and evaluation distribution. Hyperparameters transferred across models and SAE architectures produced substantial differences in effective sparsity.
record.rows_left_out: No neuron-pole audit or neuron-explanation result is reported. The paper reports additional SAE analyses and supporting metrics in Appendices D–J, but these concern SAE features rather than the neuron-pole quantities in the claim.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles. The Qwen3-32B result (r11) is on public BatchTopK SAE features, not neurons.
No neuron-pole shares in any model; the larger-model panels are SAE features.
No vision models, InceptionV1, cat-and-car neuron, or recursive generalization.
No neuron interpretability as a function of architecture or tools. Its architecture effects are SAE-architecture effects on SAE features.
No attribution graphs over model neurons and no comparison with replacement models.
Held-out ranking of explanations is applied only to SAE features, never to neurons.
Simulation-style scoring is not applied to neurons. The Bills et al. neuron score share is only cited (Appendix E.2).

record.verdict_notes: The paper is about SAE dictionaries, and its claims about neurons are motivating assumptions. Rows r1–r12 correctly carry versions ["none"]. Their states describe the SAE Q1-deficit finding, not any claim version. The J.2 result (binary vs DAME) could be added as a row for the fits_no_version finding. The cited neuron statistics in Appendix E (Bills et al., Templeton et al.) are correctly excluded as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate shares with one, two, or unknown jobs.
Larger-model results are about SAE features, not neuron poles; they do not test whether neuron-pole shares generalize across architectures or scale.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 or the cat-and-car neuron, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not test neuron interpretability in InceptionV1-sized vision models or the stated estimates about architecture, tools, and interpretability.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons or compare them with a replacement model and reconstruction error.
DAME tests explanations of SAE features, not explanations of neurons; it does not directly test the stated neuron claim.
Automated scoring is applied to SAE feature explanations, not neuron explanations; the paper does not report the share of neurons achieving good scores.
